title: Bix, the Whiteman and Goldkette sidemen, and leaving the NORK behind
summary: Freeman says Bix is hard to hear through sidemen who were not true jazzmen, and the Chicagoans never went back to the NORK after Oliver.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: For the first time. There was no one -- of course, there was the great Bix and here unfortunately we did not -- the kids, and the young people listen to Bix today and even many musicians listen to Bix today,

and it is difficult to listen to Bix through all the other players because those players were not essentially jazzmen. They were men in the Whiteman band and in the Goldkette band who could read anything. They were fine disciplined musicians, but Bix out of a sense of loyalty, you know, playing with the men in the band used them on his records. They were not really, and I hope I am not being unfair when I say this, that they were not really jazzmen who lived the jazz music as did Louis and King and Bix and many of the greats, Dave and Kenny Clarke Tough, Benny Carter and a few people like that who were later to become --

I think that we then, as I said, never went back or as I meant to say, we never went back to the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, after hearing the King Oliver Band, because we realized that in hearing the King Oliver Band, we were listening to the real thing.
